q.intro.text: A drawing of a skateboard is four inches long. The actual skateboard is thirty-two inches long. A scale compares the two lengths, drawing first. Which scale fits this drawing? Pick one, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one. The picture moves first, then the maths on the board.

e.step0.text: Length goes with length, width with width. The drawing's four inches match the actual thirty-two inches, and one inch matches eight inches.

e.step1.text: Lay the drawing's length along the actual board. Eight copies fill it. Thirty-two divided by four is eight, so the actual board is eight times as long. Not twenty-eight times. Twenty-eight is only how much longer it is.

e.step2.text: One factor has to work for every length. The width. Eight copies of one inch fill eight inches, and eight divided by one is eight again. So the drawing is to scale.

e.step3.text: Write the scale drawing first, actual second, in one unit. Four to thirty-two is one to eight. It says one inch on the drawing stands for eight inches of skateboard.

e.why.text: Quick check. Why is the scale one to eight, and not one to twenty-eight?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. Eight copies of the drawing fill the actual board, both ways. A scale counts copies.

e.why.diff.text: Twenty-eight is the difference, thirty-two minus four. But one inch on the drawing does not stand for twenty-nine inches. It stands for eight.

e.why.few.text: Every length has to fit the same factor. If the width needed another one, the drawing would be stretched.

t.intro.text: Now a laptop. The drawing is six centimeters by four centimeters. The actual laptop is thirty centimeters by twenty centimeters. I'll do the first two steps, then it's your turn.

t.given.text: Five copies of the drawing's six centimeters fill the actual thirty centimeters. The actual length is five times as long.

t.wid.text: Now the width. The actual width is how many times as long as the drawing's width?

t.wid.ok.text: Right. Twenty divided by four is five. Five copies fill the width too. One factor, both ways.

t.wid.diff.text: Sixteen is how much longer, twenty minus four. How many copies of four centimeters fit in twenty centimeters?

t.wid.rev.text: That compares the drawing with the laptop. The actual width is the long one. How many times as long is it?

t.wid.len.text: Twenty centimeters is the actual width itself. How many times does four centimeters fit into it?

t.wid.miss.text: Count copies. How many fours make twenty? Try again.

t.scale.text: Write the scale, drawing to actual, in the form one to n.

t.scale.ok.text: Right. Six to thirty is one to five. One centimeter on the drawing stands for five centimeters of laptop.

t.scale.rev.text: Drawing first. The drawing is the small one. One to five, not five to one.

t.scale.diff.text: Twenty-four is the difference, thirty minus six. A scale is times as long. Thirty divided by six.

t.scale.equiv.text: Six to thirty is the same comparison. Now make the drawing part one. Divide both parts by six.

t.scale.one.text: You divided the six by six, but not the thirty. Divide both parts. Thirty divided by six is five.

t.scale.miss.text: Drawing to actual is six to thirty. Divide both parts by six.

t.empty.text: Type a number in each box first.

q.cb.right.text: At the start you picked one to eight, and you were right. Now you can show why. Eight copies, both ways.

q.cb.diff.text: At the start you picked one to twenty-eight. That is the difference, thirty-two minus four. A scale counts copies. Thirty-two divided by four is eight, so one to eight.

q.cb.rev.text: At the start you picked eight to one. That puts the actual board first. Drawing first, so one to eight.

q.cb.none.text: A scale counts how many copies of the drawing make the actual length, drawing first.

p.intro.text: A floor plan is drawn at one to one hundred. On the plan, the hallway is five centimeters long and two centimeters wide. Sam says, the scale is one to one hundred, so the hallway is one hundred centimeters long. Is Sam right?

p.build.no.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.build.yes.text: Let's test it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true, and see where it leads.

p.c1.text: Right. Each centimeter of the plan stands for one hundred centimeters of hallway. One hundred is a factor, not a length.

p.c2.text: Right. Sam's one hundred centimeters is only the first centimeter of the plan. The whole hallway is five times one hundred, five hundred centimeters.

p.c3.text: Right. The width uses the same factor. Two times one hundred is two hundred centimeters. Different lengths, one scale.

p.done.text: That's a proof. Three claims, each with its reason, and the picture backs every one. A scale is a factor. It multiplies every length on the plan.

p.chip.len.text: That is Sam's slip. One hundred is not the length of any wall. It multiplies the lengths on the plan.

p.chip.seg.text: One plan, one scale. Every length on it uses the same factor, long or short.

p.chip.unit.text: In inches both lengths change together, so it stays one to one hundred. And it is not the reason for this line.

p.chip.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?
